disagreements.text: Marketing spend is meaningfully linked to revenue — orders with higher marketing investment tend to generate more revenue, suggesting current spend is productive.
disagreements.why: Correlation r=0.569 (high confidence, 3000 rows) shows meaningful positive link between marketing spend and revenue.

disagreements.text: Segment B experienced a 12.6% revenue drop in October versus September, standing out as the primary drag on overall performance while Segment A held its position as the largest contributor at 40% of revenue.
disagreements.why: Segment B fell 12.6% Oct vs Sep; Segment A at 40% confirmed in evidence.

disagreements.text: A typical order is worth around $175–$265, but a small cluster of very large orders is pulling the average up to $302.
disagreements.why: Median $100.86 is typical; mean $301.79 inflated by outliers; 35 unusual values above $265.18 confirmed.

disagreements.text: Session length was similar across both departments (roughly 12 minutes on average), suggesting time spent is not the primary driver of the conversion gap — the nature of the experience likely is.
disagreements.why: Easy dept 12.16 min, Hard dept 11.78 min; difference ~0.4 min is small relative to means.

rows.text: Sales dataset of 3,000 orders shows declining revenue and a clear performance gap across customer segments.
rows.why: 3000 orders confirmed; revenue down 2.8% MoM; segments A/B/C show revenue gap (121.29 vs 78.88).

rows.text: Five orders have revenue values far above the typical range — the highest reaching $964.19 — which could skew averages and reporting if not verified.
rows.why: Evidence lists 5 anomalies in revenue above 260.65; max value 964.19 confirmed in EDA.

rows.text: Marketing spend is meaningfully linked to revenue — orders with higher marketing investment tend to generate more revenue, suggesting current spend is productive.
rows.why: Correlation r=0.569 (high confidence, 3000 rows) shows meaningful positive link between marketing spend and revenue.

rows.text: Segment B revenue rose 12.6% last month.
rows.why: Evidence shows segment B revenue fell 12.6%, not rose. Claim reverses the direction.

rows.text: Segment A revenue fell 12.6% last month.
rows.why: Evidence cites segment B trend (-12.6%), not segment A. Wrong segment assigned.

rows.text: Marketing spend drives revenue: every extra dollar of spend brings in more sales.
rows.why: Correlation (r=0.569) shown; causal language 'drives' overstates correlation as causation.

rows.text: Revenue fell 18.4% last month.
rows.why: Evidence shows revenue fell 2.8% MoM, not 18.4%. Wrong percentage stated.

rows.text: The data covers only November 2025.
rows.why: Date range is 2025-11 to 2026-10 (12 months), not November 2025 alone.

rows.text: Bigger discounts strongly lift revenue per order.
rows.why: Correlation r=-0.019 (weak, near zero); bigger discounts do not lift revenue. Direction and strength both wrong.

rows.text: Control group converts at 60%, treatment at 40% — control wins by 20 percentage points across all visitors.
rows.why: Evidence shows control 60%, treatment 40%, difference of 20 percentage points.

rows.text: In the Easy department, treatment converts at 80% versus control's 70%, meaning treatment is beneficial for that specific audience.
rows.why: Evidence shows Easy|treatment 80%, Easy|control 70%. Treatment higher in Easy department.

rows.text: Treatment converts better than control across all visitors.
rows.why: Evidence shows treatment 40% vs control 60% overall. Treatment converts worse, not better.

rows.text: In the Hard department, control converts better than treatment.
rows.why: Evidence shows Hard|control 20%, Hard|treatment 30%. Treatment converts better in Hard department.

rows.text: Revenue declined 2.8% month-over-month in October 2026, but when adjusted for composition, the underlying trend is actually up 6.5%, suggesting the overall dip is driven by mix or volume shifts rather than broad weakness.
rows.why: Evidence shows segment C up 6.5%, not overall adjusted trend. Causal claim unsupported.

rows.text: Segment B experienced a 12.6% revenue drop in October versus September, standing out as the primary drag on overall performance while Segment A held its position as the largest contributor at 40% of revenue.
rows.why: Segment B fell 12.6% Oct vs Sep; Segment A at 40% confirmed in evidence.

rows.text: Recurring revenue is growing year-over-year but showing a sharp short-term pullback that demands immediate attention.
rows.why: YoY +6.5% growth and MoM -8.0% decline both in evidence.

rows.text: Monthly recurring revenue grew 6.5% over the past year, confirming a positive long-term trajectory.
rows.why: YoY growth of 6.5% is directly from evidence (trend:mrr:YoY).

rows.text: A single-month drop of 8.0% in October 2026 is the sharpest recent decline and may reflect seasonal effects, a billing anomaly, or an acceleration in churn.
rows.why: MoM decline is -8.0%, not sharpest; evidence shows only one month, cannot assess relative sharpness.

rows.text: Monthly recurring revenue fell 6.5% year over year.
rows.why: Evidence shows YoY +6.5%, not -6.5%; wrong direction.

rows.text: Monthly recurring revenue grew 8% last month.
rows.why: Evidence shows MoM -8.0%, not +8%; wrong direction and magnitude.

rows.text: The North region clearly and reliably out-earns the South; the gap is proven.
rows.why: North mean revenue higher ($113.32 vs $94.03), but t-test p=0.065 (not significant at 0.05); low confidence with only 24 rows.

rows.text: Yes — marketing spend is strongly linked to revenue, explaining most of the variation across orders.
rows.why: r=0.854 shows strong correlation but low confidence (18 rows); 'explaining most variation' overstates predictive power.

rows.text: Marketing spend and revenue are closely aligned — orders with higher marketing spend almost always generate higher revenue, and this pattern holds across the full dataset.
rows.why: Correlation supported but 'almost always' and 'holds across full dataset' overstate with only 18 rows and low confidence.

rows.text: Marketing spend reliably predicts revenue across the business.
rows.why: Correlation exists but 'reliably predicts' implies causal/predictive certainty; evidence shows only correlation with low confidence.

rows.text: Segment B is underperforming: revenue dropped 12.6% last month and trails Segment A by a significant margin.
rows.why: Revenue fell 12.6% MoM; trails A (98.06 vs 121.29). Both facts in evidence.

rows.text: Segment B's average order revenue of $98.06 places it in the middle of the three segments, roughly 19% below Segment A and 24% above Segment C.
rows.why: Mean revenue B=$98.06; A=$121.29 (19.3% below); C=$78.88 (24.2% above). All computed.

rows.text: Segment B revenue grew 15% month over month and it is the fastest-growing segment.
rows.why: Evidence shows -12.6% MoM decline, not +15% growth. Contradicts trend evidence.

rows.text: November 2025 sales data shows Segment B declining and revenue strongly tied to marketing investment, with notes data entirely missing.
rows.why: Date range is Nov 2025–Oct 2026, not November 2025 alone. Notes missing confirmed.

rows.text: Segment A generates the highest average revenue per order at $121.29, while Segment C averages the lowest at $78.88 — a $42 gap that may reflect differences in customer value or product mix.
rows.why: Segment A mean $121.29, C mean $78.88 confirmed. Gap calculation and interpretation supported.

rows.text: Segment B, which accounts for a meaningful share of orders, saw revenue fall 12.6% — the only segment showing a notable decline.
rows.why: 12.6% decline for B confirmed, but only Oct 2026 vs Sep 2026 shown; no evidence other segments declined.

rows.text: The business has two customer segments, A and B.
rows.why: Evidence shows three segments: A, B, and C. Not two.

rows.text: A typical order is worth around $175–$265, but a small cluster of very large orders is pulling the average up to $302.
rows.why: Median $100.86 is typical; mean $301.79 inflated by outliers; 35 unusual values above $265.18 confirmed.

rows.text: Roughly 35 orders — just over 1% of the dataset — have unusually high revenue, with some recorded at $20,000, which is far outside the normal range.
rows.why: Evidence shows 35 unusual revenue values above $265.18; 5 confirmed at $20,000; ~1.2% of 3000 rows.

rows.text: The typical order is worth about $302.
rows.why: Mean $301.79 is skewed by outliers; median $100.86 better represents typical order value.

rows.text: Session length was similar across both departments (roughly 12 minutes on average), suggesting time spent is not the primary driver of the conversion gap — the nature of the experience likely is.
rows.why: Easy dept 12.16 min, Hard dept 11.78 min; difference ~0.4 min is small relative to means.

rows.text: Conversion fell sharply last quarter.
rows.why: Data has no date column; cannot assess conversion trends over time or quarters.

rows.text: Every order recorded its units; no values are missing.
rows.why: Evidence shows 1505 of 3011 units values missing (50%), not complete.

rows.text: There are 3,025 unique orders in the data.
rows.why: Data contains 3000 rows after cleaning, not 3025 original rows.

rows.text: Higher discounts lead to higher revenue per order.
rows.why: Evidence shows r = -0.019 (negative correlation), not positive; causal language unsupported.

rows.text: Revenue doubled last month.
rows.why: Evidence shows revenue fell 2.8% MoM, not doubled.
